title: Balfour to Partition: The Mandate Years
overview: This chapter opens with the Balfour Declaration of 2 November 1917, in which Britain's foreign secretary declared support for "a national home for the Jewish people" in Palestine, then Ottoman territory being conquered by British forces. The San Remo conference assigned the Mandate to Britain in April 1920, and the League of Nations Council approved its text, incorporating the Balfour pledge, in July 1922. Under British administration Jewish immigration and land purchases grew and Zionist institutions developed, while a Palestinian Arab national movement organised against both Zionism and British rule. Violence broke out in 1920, 1921 and 1929, and the Arab revolt of 1936-1939 was suppressed by British forces. The 1939 White Paper capped Jewish immigration as persecution intensified in Europe, provoking Zionist opposition; after 1945 Jewish underground groups attacked British targets while Holocaust survivors sought entry. Britain referred the question to the United Nations in February 1947, and the UN Special Committee on Palestine recommended partition in August. Throughout the period Britain held territorial control as mandatory power. Israelis generally describe the era as international recognition of Jewish national rights and the building of a state-in-waiting. Palestinians generally describe it as the imposition of a settler-colonial project on a country whose Arab majority was never consulted. The UN's own historical account notes that the Mandate embodied the Balfour pledge while the League Covenant's principle of self-determination was not applied to Palestine's inhabitants.

title: Partition, War, and the Nakba
overview: On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 181 by 33 votes to 13, recommending partition of Palestine into a Jewish state, an Arab state and an internationally administered Jerusalem. Jewish leaders accepted the plan; Palestinian Arab leaders and the Arab League rejected it, and intercommunal fighting began at once. As British forces withdrew, Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948; armies from Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon entered the next day. Two UN truces and the assassination of mediator Folke Bernadotte punctuated the war, which ended with armistice agreements signed between February and July 1949. Israel emerged holding about 78 percent of Mandate Palestine, more than the plan allotted; Transjordan held the West Bank and East Jerusalem, and Egypt administered the Gaza Strip. No Arab state was established. Britannica records estimates of Palestinian Arabs displaced ranging from about 520,000 to one million, with broad consensus that the figure exceeded 700,000; UN General Assembly Resolution 194 of December 1948 affirmed that refugees wishing to return should be permitted to do so or be compensated. Israelis generally call this the War of Independence, a defensive struggle for survival after Arab rejection of partition. Palestinians generally call it the Nakba ("catastrophe"), the 1948 Palestinian displacement in which hundreds of villages were depopulated. The UN regards the refugee question as unresolved and a matter of continuing international responsibility.

title: Armistice Lines and the Suez Crisis
overview: The 1949 armistice lines, later called the Green Line, defined the map for eighteen years without becoming recognised borders. Jordan formally annexed the West Bank in April 1950, a step recognised only by Britain and Pakistan; Egypt administered the Gaza Strip through a military governor without annexing it; and UNRWA began operating in 1950 for registered refugees across the region. Cross-border infiltration and Israeli reprisal raids marked the early 1950s. After Egypt nationalised the Suez Canal in July 1956, Israel invaded Sinai on 29 October in coordination with Britain and France, whose forces landed at Port Said in early November. Under US and Soviet pressure, and with the first UN Emergency Force (UNEF) deployed, Britain and France withdrew by December 1956 and Israel completed its withdrawal from Sinai and Gaza by March 1957. The Arab League founded the PLO in 1964. In May 1967 Egypt requested UNEF's departure, moved forces into Sinai and closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping, precipitating the June war. Israelis generally describe the period as one of encirclement, fedayeen raids and blockade threatening a young state. Palestinians generally describe it as years of dispersal and statelessness under neighbouring Arab governments, with the refugee question frozen. The UN maintained truce supervision through UNTSO and treated the armistice lines as provisional pending a negotiated peace.

title: Six-Day War to the October War
overview: On 5 June 1967 Israel launched air strikes on Egypt after weeks of mobilisation and Egypt's closure of the Straits of Tiran; within six days it had captured the Sinai Peninsula and Gaza Strip from Egypt, the West Bank including East Jerusalem from Jordan, and the Golan Heights from Syria. Israel extended its jurisdiction to East Jerusalem that month and began establishing settlements in the newly held territories, which the UN regards as Israeli-occupied. Security Council Resolution 242 of 22 November 1967 called for withdrawal "from territories occupied in the recent conflict" together with every state's right to live in peace within secure and recognised boundaries; its precise meaning remains disputed. A war of attrition followed along the Suez Canal. On 6 October 1973 Egypt and Syria attacked on Yom Kippur; after early Arab advances and Israeli counter-offensives, Resolution 338 brought a ceasefire on 26 October. US shuttle diplomacy produced an Egyptian-Israeli disengagement in January 1974 and the Israeli-Syrian agreement of 31 May 1974, which created a UN-monitored buffer zone on the Golan (UNDOF). Israelis generally regard 1967 as a defensive victory that reunified Jerusalem and 1973 as a costly test of survival. Palestinians generally regard 1967 as the Naksa ("setback") that placed the remaining Palestinian territories under Israeli military control and displaced hundreds of thousands more. The UN treats the territories captured in 1967 as occupied and does not recognise their annexation.

title: Camp David and the Lebanon War
overview: Diplomacy and war ran in parallel. Egyptian President Anwar Sadat addressed the Knesset in November 1977, and in September 1978 Sadat, Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin and US President Jimmy Carter concluded the Camp David Accords: a framework for an Egyptian-Israeli treaty and a separate framework proposing Palestinian autonomy in the West Bank and Gaza. The treaty signed in March 1979 was the first between Israel and an Arab state; Israel completed its withdrawal from Sinai in April 1982. The autonomy framework was never implemented, and settlement building in the West Bank and Gaza accelerated under Likud governments. The PLO, based in Lebanon since 1970, fought Israel across the border; after a 1978 Israeli incursion the UN created UNIFIL. On 6 June 1982 Israel invaded Lebanon, besieged West Beirut and forced the PLO leadership's evacuation to Tunis in August. In September, after the assassination of President-elect Bashir Gemayel, Lebanese Phalangist militiamen killed hundreds of Palestinian and Lebanese civilians in the Sabra and Shatila camps while Israeli forces controlled the area; Israel's Kahan Commission found indirect Israeli responsibility. Israel pulled back to a self-declared "security zone" in southern Lebanon in 1985, where the newly formed Hezbollah fought it. Israelis generally describe the era as peace with Egypt and a necessary campaign against PLO attacks from Lebanon. Palestinians generally describe it as exclusion from decisions about their future and the loss of their Lebanese base. The UN condemned the Sabra and Shatila killings in Security Council Resolution 521.

title: First Intifada and the Road to Oslo
overview: The first intifada began on 9 December 1987 in Gaza's Jabalia camp after an Israeli vehicle struck vans carrying Palestinian workers, and spread across the Gaza Strip and West Bank as a largely popular uprising of strikes, boycotts, stone-throwing and civil disobedience. Hamas was founded the same month by members of the Muslim Brotherhood. Israel responded with mass arrests, curfews, deportations and live fire; B'Tselem recorded about 1,100 Palestinians killed by Israeli security forces and about 160 Israelis killed by Palestinians between December 1987 and September 1993, alongside Palestinians killed by other Palestinians as suspected collaborators. In November 1988 the Palestine National Council in Algiers declared a State of Palestine and accepted Resolutions 242 and 338, opening a dialogue with the United States. The PLO's alignment with Iraq in the 1991 Gulf War weakened it; afterwards the United States and Soviet Union convened the Madrid Conference in October 1991, bringing Israel into direct talks with Syria, Lebanon and a joint Jordanian-Palestinian delegation. Public negotiations stalled, but secret Israeli-PLO talks in Norway produced a breakthrough in August 1993. Territorial control did not change. Israelis generally describe the intifada as violent unrest that nonetheless persuaded many that ruling the territories indefinitely was untenable. Palestinians generally describe it as a grassroots national awakening that forced their cause onto the diplomatic agenda. The UN General Assembly acknowledged the Palestinian declaration in December 1988.

title: The Oslo Process
overview: On 13 September 1993 Israel and the PLO signed the Declaration of Principles at the White House, following letters in which the PLO recognised Israel's right to exist and renounced violence, and Israel recognised the PLO as the representative of the Palestinian people. The accords created a Palestinian Authority with limited self-rule for a five-year interim period, deferring Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, borders and security to permanent-status talks. The Gaza-Jericho agreement of May 1994 brought the first Israeli withdrawals; Jordan and Israel signed a peace treaty in October 1994; and the Interim Agreement (Oslo II, September 1995) divided the West Bank into Area A (Palestinian civil and security control), Area B (Palestinian civil control, Israeli security control) and Area C (full Israeli control, about 60 percent of the territory). Rabin was assassinated by an Israeli opponent of the accords in November 1995. Suicide bombings by Hamas and Islamic Jihad, Israeli closures and continued settlement growth eroded support on both sides; Netanyahu's government slowed implementation, though the Hebron and Wye River agreements of 1997-1998 transferred further territory. The Camp David summit of July 2000 between Barak, Arafat and Clinton ended without agreement, each side blaming the other. Israelis generally describe Oslo as a genuine offer of compromise undermined by Palestinian violence and rejection. Palestinians generally describe it as an interim arrangement that entrenched fragmentation and settlement expansion without delivering statehood. The UN welcomed the accords while maintaining that permanent status must rest on Resolutions 242 and 338.

title: Second Intifada, Barrier, and Disengagement
overview: The second intifada began on 28 September 2000 after Ariel Sharon's visit to the Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif and the deadly clashes that followed; it quickly became an armed conflict. Palestinian groups carried out suicide bombings and shootings inside Israel, while Israel mounted large incursions into Palestinian cities (Operation Defensive Shield, April 2002) and targeted killings. B'Tselem recorded more than 3,000 Palestinians killed by Israeli security forces and around 1,000 Israelis killed by Palestinians between September 2000 and the end of 2005. Israel began building the West Bank barrier in 2002, much of its route inside the West Bank; the International Court of Justice advised on 9 July 2004 that construction in occupied territory was contrary to international law. Arafat died in November 2004 and Mahmoud Abbas was elected in January 2005. In August-September 2005 Israel unilaterally withdrew its settlers and forces from the Gaza Strip and four northern West Bank settlements, retaining control of Gaza's airspace, coastline and most crossings. Hamas won the January 2006 Palestinian legislative elections, prompting an international aid boycott and Fatah-Hamas clashes; in June 2007 Hamas seized Gaza by force, leaving the Palestinian Authority governing only parts of the West Bank. Israelis generally describe the period as a terror war that justified the security fence and disengagement. Palestinians generally describe it as resistance to a stalled peace process and the separation wall's confiscation of land. The UN endorsed the ICJ opinion and called for barrier construction to stop.

title: Blockade, Gaza Wars, and the Abraham Accords
overview: After Hamas took control of Gaza in June 2007, Israel, with Egyptian cooperation at Rafah, imposed a land, sea and air blockade that the UN's OCHA describes as restricting movement of people and goods to the point of "de-development"; Israel says the measures prevent arms from reaching Hamas. Rocket fire from Gaza and Israeli air strikes produced repeated major escalations: Cast Lead (December 2008-January 2009), Pillar of Defense (November 2012), Protective Edge (July-August 2014) and the May 2021 escalation. B'Tselem documented 1,385 Palestinians and 13 Israelis killed in 2008-09, while Israel put Palestinian deaths at about 1,166; OCHA counted 2,251 Palestinians and 73 Israelis killed in 2014. In the West Bank the Palestinian Authority governed enclaves in Areas A and B while settlements grew and the barrier was extended; Palestine became a UN non-member observer state in November 2012, and US-led talks in 2010 and 2013-2014 failed. The United States moved its embassy to Jerusalem in 2018 and brokered the Abraham Accords in September 2020, normalising Israel's relations with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. Violence in the West Bank climbed sharply in 2022-2023. Israelis generally describe the period as managing a terror threat from a Hamas-ruled enclave while widening peace with Arab states. Palestinians generally describe it as sixteen years of siege, political division between Gaza and the West Bank, and abandonment by normalising governments. The UN repeatedly called for the blockade to be lifted and settlement activity to cease.

title: October 7 and the Gaza War
overview: On 7 October 2023 Hamas-led militants breached the Gaza perimeter under rocket cover and attacked communities, army bases and a music festival in southern Israel, killing about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, according to Israeli authorities, and taking 251 hostages into Gaza. Israel declared war and began an air campaign, followed on 27 October by a ground invasion of northern Gaza that later extended to Khan Younis and, from May 2024, Rafah, where it seized the Egyptian border corridor and the Rafah crossing. A week-long truce in late November 2023 exchanged 105 hostages for 240 Palestinian prisoners. By mid-August 2024 the Gaza Health Ministry reported more than 40,000 Palestinians killed, a figure UN agencies cite while Israel disputes its composition; OCHA estimated 1.9 million people displaced. Hezbollah opened a limited front from 8 October 2023, Houthi forces attacked Red Sea shipping, and Iran and Israel exchanged direct strikes in April 2024. South Africa brought a genocide case at the International Court of Justice, which ordered provisional measures in January, March and May 2024; the ICC prosecutor sought warrants for Israeli and Hamas leaders in May. Israelis generally describe the war as a defensive response to the deadliest massacre of Jews since the Holocaust, aimed at destroying Hamas and freeing hostages. Palestinians generally describe it as genocide and a second Nakba inflicted on a besieged population. The UN Secretary-General called the 7 October attack unjustifiable and the Gaza campaign a humanitarian catastrophe, repeatedly demanding a ceasefire.

title: Lebanon, Iran, and Regional Escalation
overview: On 17-18 September 2024 pagers and radios used by Hezbollah members exploded across Lebanon, killing dozens and injuring thousands according to Lebanese authorities, in an operation widely attributed to Israel. Israel killed Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah in Beirut on 27 September and sent ground forces into southern Lebanon on 1 October; Iran fired about 180 missiles at Israel that day. Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was killed in Rafah on 16 October. A US- and French-brokered Lebanon ceasefire took effect on 27 November. When the Assad government fell on 8 December, Israel moved troops into the UN-monitored Golan buffer zone and Mount Hermon, which the UN said violated the 1974 agreement. A Gaza ceasefire began on 19 January 2025: 33 hostages were exchanged for nearly 1,900 Palestinian prisoners. Israel halted aid entry in early March and resumed strikes on 18 March, killing more than 400 people that day according to the Gaza Health Ministry; a US- and Israel-backed aid foundation began distributions in late May amid deadly shootings near its sites. On 13 June Israel attacked Iran's nuclear and military sites, the United States struck Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan on 22 June, and a ceasefire took effect on 24 June; Iran's Health Ministry reported more than 900 Iranians killed and Israeli authorities 28 Israelis. Israelis generally describe these months as dismantling Iran's "ring of fire". Palestinians and Lebanese generally describe them as expanding Israeli occupation and collective punishment. The UN warned of regional war and of famine in Gaza.

title: The October 2025 Ceasefire and After
overview: In August 2025 the IPC confirmed famine in Gaza Governorate as Israel moved to seize Gaza City; Israel's 9 September strike on Hamas leaders in Doha was widely condemned, and on 21-22 September Britain, Canada, Australia and France recognised a State of Palestine. Trump's 20-point plan of 29 September produced a ceasefire on 10 October 2025 and the release of the 20 living hostages for nearly 2,000 Palestinian prisoners and detainees. Security Council Resolution 2803 (17 November) endorsed the plan, a Trump-chaired Board of Peace and an International Stabilization Force. Israeli forces held more than half of Gaza behind a "yellow line"; Gaza's Health Ministry reported over 1,100 Palestinians killed since the ceasefire and over 73,000 since October 2023. On 28 February 2026 the United States and Israel attacked Iran, killing Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei; Iran struck back and closed the Strait of Hormuz, Hezbollah opened fire on 2 March, and Israel invaded southern Lebanon, where the Lebanese Health Ministry counted more than 2,000 killed by mid-April. A Pakistan-mediated ceasefire began on 8 April; a June memorandum collapsed into renewed strikes in July. On 31 July Trump announced a Hamas disarmament deal; Israel refused any withdrawal until Hamas disarms. Israel approved 34 new West Bank settlements in April amid record settler violence recorded by OCHA. Israelis generally describe the period as recovering hostages without ceding Gaza to armed Hamas. Palestinians generally describe it as occupation continuing under a nominal ceasefire. The UN calls the ceasefire fragile and Gaza's needs immense.
